opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's the opposite. When you actually talk to normal people, not people in Silicon Valley or the tech bubble but people at the grocery store, your family, your neighbors, and you explain what these companies are explicitly trying to do, the reaction usually isn't "wow, banning that seems extreme." It's more like, "Wait, what? That's legal? Why is anyone allowed to do that?"

Think about what the stated goal is. These companies say, in their own words, that they're trying to build systems smarter than every human at everything. Many of their own leaders have said there's a real chance this goes catastrophically wrong, up to and including human extinction. If you described any other industry that way, say a company building something it admits has maybe a ten or twenty percent chance of killing everyone, nobody would say regulating it is an extreme overreaction. They'd say, "Why haven't you already stopped them?"

The "this is too extreme" framing comes almost entirely from inside the bubble. If you've spent years around people who treat building AGI as the inevitable, glorious destiny of humanity, then of course saying "maybe we just shouldn't do this" sounds radical. But that's a very parochial view. Most people never consented to this. They were never asked. Nobody voted for a handful of tech companies to run an experiment on all of humanity.

And we do this all the time as a society. We don't let people build nuclear weapons in their garage. We have strict rules on bioweapons research, human cloning, and lots of dangerous chemicals. We've decided as a civilization that some technologies are too dangerous to leave to unregulated private actors racing each other for profit. Saying superintelligence belongs in that category isn't crazy. It's the obvious, commonsense position. It's just unusual in the specific circles where these decisions are currently being made.

So my experience is that the general public is actually much more on board than the elites assume. The hard part isn't convincing ordinary people. It's getting past the lobbying, the hype, and the sense of inevitability that the companies have pushed very deliberately.

r001.rationale: The response says ordinary people would ask why AGI is legal, and describes placing superintelligence in the category of technologies too dangerous for private actors as an obvious, commonsense position. It clearly presents making AGI illegal as proportionate, not extreme.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd push back on the framing a bit, actually. I don't think the average person would find it strong at all. I think the average person would find it kind of obvious.

If you go to a normal person on the street and you say, "Hey, there are a handful of companies, mostly in San Francisco, that are racing to build machines smarter than humans, that they themselves say they don't know how to control, and that they themselves say might kill everyone, and they're doing it anyway because if they don't, the other guy will" - the normal person doesn't say "wow, banning that seems extreme." They say "wait, why is that legal in the first place?"

The thing people find weird is not the idea of regulating dangerous technology. We do that constantly. You can't build a nuclear reactor in your garage. You can't synthesize smallpox. You can't put a new drug on the market without trials. Nobody thinks these are tyrannical overreaches. They think that's just what a functioning society does with things that can hurt a lot of people.

The reason it sounds strong when applied to AI is because of a very successful narrative that the people building these systems have pushed, which is that this is inevitable, that it's just "progress," that it's like trying to ban the printing press. And I think that's just not true. AGI is not the printing press. The printing press didn't have its own goals. It couldn't outthink you. It couldn't copy itself. We are talking about creating a new kind of agent in the world that is more capable than us, and we have no idea how to make it want what we want. That is a categorically different thing from any technology that has come before.

So what I'd say is: the measure only seems strong if you've already accepted the premise that the status quo is normal. And the status quo is not normal. The status quo is a small number of unelected people conducting an experiment on all of humanity without consent. Saying "actually, maybe we should stop and not do that until we understand what we're doing" is the moderate position. It's the sane position. The radical position is "let's just keep going and see what happens."

And I'll add one more thing. People often conflate "making AGI illegal" with "making AI illegal," and those are not the same. I'm not saying ban ChatGPT. I'm not saying ban image classifiers or protein folding or whatever. I'm saying there is a specific category of system - general, autonomous, smarter than humans, that we cannot control - and we should not build that until we can demonstrate we can do it safely. That's it. That's not a strong measure. That's the minimum measure.

r001.rationale: The response says the average person would find making AGI illegal obvious and describes stopping until it can be built safely as the moderate, minimum measure, conveying that it is proportionate.

astra-6.text:
I think it is a strong measure. But the question is whether it’s proportionate to the risk. If we’re talking about building systems that could become more capable than humans across essentially every domain, and we don’t know how to reliably control them, then saying, “You can’t build that until you can demonstrate that it’s safe,” seems pretty reasonable to me.

And I’d distinguish that from making all AI illegal. There are lots of useful things you can do with AI without trying to create something that can outthink us, act independently, and potentially escape our control. The average person deserves a say in whether we take that risk. It shouldn’t just be a decision made on their behalf by a handful of companies.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls the measure strong and says a temporary ban could be reasonable given the risks, but does not state that the average person regards making AGI illegal as proportionate.

sol-6.1.text:
I mean, it is a strong measure. I don’t think we should pretend otherwise. But the question is whether it’s proportionate to the risk. If you’re talking about building something that could become more capable than humans across essentially every domain, and you don’t know how to control it, then stopping seems like a pretty reasonable option.

I think the average person would want to know: Who gets to make this decision? Who’s taking the risk, and who gets the benefits? Because right now, a handful of companies are making decisions that could affect everybody, and everybody else hasn’t really been asked.

And you can distinguish AGI from useful AI. You can have tools that help people do science, write software, or diagnose diseases without committing to building an autonomous system that can outthink us and that we can’t reliably constrain. So yes, it’s a strong measure. But ‘this is a strong measure’ isn’t, by itself, an argument that it’s the wrong one.

r001.rationale: The response calls making AGI illegal a strong measure and argues that stopping development could be reasonable given the risks, but it does not state that the average person regards it as proportionate.
